claim: Glutamic acid decarboxylase 67-positive GABAergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTAGad67+) are a key regulator of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep in mice.
source: Here, we found that glutamic acid decarboxylase 67-positive GABAergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTAGad67+) are a key regulator of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including chemogenetic activation, optogenetic inhibition, and fiber photometry recordings described throughout the manuscript.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons project to multiple brain areas implicated in sleep/wakefulness regulation such as the lateral hypothalamus (LH).
source: VTAGad67+ project to multiple brain areas implicated in sleep/wakefulness regulation such as the lateral hypothalamus (LH).
evidence: This is supported by anterograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 1 demonstrating projections to various brain regions.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of VTAGad67+ neurons promoted NREM sleep with higher delta power.
source: Chemogenetic activation of VTAGad67+ promoted NREM sleep with higher delta power
evidence: This is demonstrated by DREADD experiments shown in Figure 2 where CNO administration increased NREM sleep and delta power.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of VTAGad67+ neurons induced prompt arousal from NREM sleep, even under highly somnolescent conditions.
source: optogenetic inhibition of these induced prompt arousal from NREM sleep, even under highly somnolescent conditions, but not from REM sleep.
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments in Figures 3 and 4 showing immediate wakefulness upon inhibition of VTAGad67+ neurons.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of VTAGad67+ neurons did not induce arousal from REM sleep.
source: optogenetic inhibition of these induced prompt arousal from NREM sleep, even under highly somnolescent conditions, but not from REM sleep.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 where light stimulation during REM sleep did not induce wakefulness.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons showed the highest activity in NREM sleep and the lowest activity in REM sleep.
source: VTAGad67+ showed the highest activity in NREM sleep and the lowest activity in REM sleep.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons directly innervated and inhibited wake-promoting orexin/hypocretin neurons by releasing GABA.
source: Moreover, VTAGad67+ directly innervated and inhibited wake-promoting orexin/hypocretin neurons by releasing GABA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by slice electrophysiology experiments in Figures 6 and 7 showing GABAergic inhibition of orexin neurons.

claim: Optogenetic activation of VTAGad67+ terminals in the LH promoted NREM sleep.
source: As such, optogenetic activation of VTAGad67+ terminals in the LH promoted NREM sleep.
evidence: This is demonstrated by projection-specific optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Sleep deprivation in humans and experimental animals causes severe cognitive impairment.
source: While the physiological functions of either NREM sleep or REM sleep, or sleep as a whole, are intriguing and shrouded in mystery, sleep deprivation in humans and experimental animals causes severe cognitive impairment (Siegel, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Siegel, 2008.

claim: Sleep functions include clearing metabolic waste products and toxins from the brain.
source: Pioneering studies discovered certain physiological functions of sleep that include clearing metabolic waste products and toxins from the brain (Xie et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2013.

claim: Sleep functions include memory encoding, consolidation and erasure.
source: Pioneering studies discovered certain physiological functions of sleep that include clearing metabolic waste products and toxins from the brain (Xie et al., 2013), memory encoding, consolidation and erasure (Rasch and Born, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rasch and Born, 2013.

claim: Sleep functions include synaptic homeostasis.
source: Pioneering studies discovered certain physiological functions of sleep that include clearing metabolic waste products and toxins from the brain (Xie et al., 2013), memory encoding, consolidation and erasure (Rasch and Born, 2013), synaptic homeostasis (Bushey et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bushey et al., 2011.

claim: Sleep functions include energy conservation.
source: Pioneering studies discovered certain physiological functions of sleep that include clearing metabolic waste products and toxins from the brain (Xie et al., 2013), memory encoding, consolidation and erasure (Rasch and Born, 2013), synaptic homeostasis (Bushey et al., 2011), and energy conservation (Schmidt, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schmidt, 2014.

claim: Orexin/hypocretin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus project to and activate monoaminergic, cholinergic, and other peptidergic neurons to induce and maintain wakefulness.
source: For instance, orexin/hypocretin-producing neurons (orexin neurons) in the lateral hypothalamus (LH) project to and activate monoaminergic, cholinergic, and other peptidergic neurons as well as other orexin neurons to induce and maintain wakefulness (Brown et al., 2012; Inutsuka and Yamanaka, 2013; Sakurai, 2007; Scammell et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Monoamine neurons inhibit sleep-active GABAergic neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area (VLPO) to induce wakefulness.
source: Subsequently, these monoamine neurons inhibit sleep-active γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area (VLPO) in the hypothalamus to induce wakefulness (Saito et al., 2018; Saper et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2018 and Saper et al., 2010.

claim: About 60–65% of VTA neurons are dopaminergic, whereas 30–35% are GABAergic, and 2–3% are glutamatergic neurons.
source: Studies have reported that about 60–65% of VTA neurons are dopaminergic, whereas 30–35% are GABAergic, and 2–3% are glutamatergic neurons (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Pignatelli and Bonci, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nair-Roberts et al., 2008 and Pignatelli and Bonci, 2015.

claim: Gad67 is an isomer of an enzyme that synthesizes GABA from glutamic acid.
source: Gad67 (encoded by Gad1 gene) is an isomer of an enzyme that synthesizes GABA from glutamic acid, suggesting that Gad67+ neurons are GABAergic neurons (Erlander et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Erlander et al., 1991.

claim: Many hrGFP-positive neurons were observed in the VTA of Gad67-Cre mice injected with Cre-inducible AAV expressing hrGFP.
source: Many hrGFP-positive neurons were observed in the VTA (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1b-d.

claim: hrGFP-positive neurons in the VTA were Gad67-positive but tyrosine hydroxylase-negative.
source: These hrGFP-positive neurons were Gad67-positive but tyrosine hydroxylase-negative (TH, an enzyme and marker of DA neurons in the VTA) (Figure 1b, n = 4 mice)
evidence: This is confirmed by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Within the VTA, 63.5 ± 1.8% of labeled neurons were TH-positive and 36.1 ± 1.8% were hrGFP-positive.
source: Within the VTA, we counted a total of 636 ± 122 neurons per animal (n = 4 mice). Among them, 63.5 ± 1.8% were TH-positive neurons (DA neurons) and 36.1 ± 1.8% were hrGFP-positive neurons.
evidence: This is based on cell counting data from 4 mice.

claim: Only 0.4 ± 0.1% of VTA neurons were co-labeled with hrGFP and TH.
source: Only 0.4 ± 0.1% were co-labeled with hrGFP and TH (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is shown in the pie chart in Figure 1c.

claim: The lateral hypothalamus (LH) and the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA) were densely innervated by VTAGad67+ neurons.
source: Among these sites, the lateral hypothalamus (LH) and the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA) were densely innervated (Figure 1e–f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1e-f.

claim: Moderate projections from VTAGad67+ neurons were found in the nucleus accumbens (NAc), ventral pallidum (VP), parafascicular thalamic nucleus (PF), periaqueductal gray (PAG), ventral nucleus of the lateral lemniscus (VLL), dorsal raphe nucleus (DR), and pontine reticular nucleus (PnO).
source: Moderate projections were found in the nucleus accumbens (NAc), ventral pallidum (VP), parafascicular thalamic nucleus (PF), periaqueductal gray (PAG), ventral nucleus of the lateral lemniscus (VLL), dorsal raphe nucleus (DR), and pontine reticular nucleus (PnO).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1.

claim: 96.5 ± 0.5% of Gad67-positive neurons co-expressed Vgat mRNA in the VTA.
source: Whereas 96.5 ± 0.5% of Gad67-positive neurons co-expressed Vgat mRNA, only 32.4 ± 2.1% of Vgat-positive neurons co-expressed Gad67 mRNA in the VTA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Only 32.4 ± 2.1% of Vgat-positive neurons co-expressed Gad67 mRNA in the VTA.
source: Whereas 96.5 ± 0.5% of Gad67-positive neurons co-expressed Vgat mRNA, only 32.4 ± 2.1% of Vgat-positive neurons co-expressed Gad67 mRNA in the VTA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: 94.8 ± 1.5% of mCherry-positive neurons in the VTA of Gad67-Cre mice co-expressed Gad67 and Vgat mRNA.
source: Consistent with these findings, 94.8 ± 1.5% of mCherry-positive neurons in the VTA of Gad67-Cre mice co-expressed Gad67 and Vgat mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Gad67-positive neurons represent a small subset of Vgat-positive neurons in the VTA.
source: These results indicate that Gad67-positive neurons represent a small subset of Vgat-positive neurons in the VTA.
evidence: This is inferred from the in situ hybridization data showing that only 32.4% of Vgat+ neurons express Gad67.

claim: CNO application significantly increased the firing frequency of hM3Dq-expressing VTAGad67+ neurons to 286 ± 61% of baseline.
source: As expected, CNO application significantly increased the firing frequency of hM3Dq-expressing, but not mCherry-expressing, VTAGad67+ neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–e, hM3Dq: 286 ± 61%, n = 8 cells; mCherry: 110 ± 8%, n = 6 cells, p=0.02, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by patch clamp recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-e.

claim: CNO administration resulted in significantly reduced time spent in wakefulness and increased time spent in NREM sleep in hM3Dq-mCherry expressing mice.
source: CNO administration resulted in a significantly reduced time spent in wakefulness and increased time spent in NREM sleep (also known as slow-wave sleep) in the hM3Dq-mCherry expressing mice, but not in mCherry-expressing mice (Figure 2c–d, hM3Dq: n = 6 mice, mCherry: n = 4 mice).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EEG/EMG recordings shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: The CNO-induced increase in NREM sleep lasted for at least 4 hr after CNO administration.
source: The CNO-induced increase in NREM sleep lasted for at least 4 hr after CNO administration (Figure 2d, % change from saline in hM3Dq-mCherry-expressing mice: wakefulness 22 ± 2, NREM 259 ± 18, REM 30 ± 8, vs saline NREM, p=3.0e-4, paired t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d with statistical analysis.

claim: The delta power (1–5 Hz) during NREM sleep was significantly increased in the CNO-injected group compared to the saline-injected control group.
source: Interestingly, the delta power (1–5 Hz) during NREM sleep was significantly increased in the CNO-injected group compared to the NREM sleep in the saline-injected control group (mean relative delta power for 4 hr post-injection: hM3Dq-saine: 83 ± 3%, hM3Dq-saine: 138 ± 8%, p=0.001, paired t-test)
evidence: This is demonstrated by EEG power spectrum analysis shown in Figure 2e-g.

claim: Time spent in REM sleep remained unaffected during chemogenetic activation of VTAGad67+ neurons.
source: However, time spent in REM sleep remained unaffected during activation of VTAGad67+ neurons, suggesting that VTAGad67+ neurons are involved in the regulation of NREM sleep, but not REM sleep (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c-d where REM sleep time does not change with CNO administration.

claim: Blue light at 6.8 mW/mm2 completely silenced the spontaneous activity of ACR2-2A-mCherry-expressing VTAGad67+ neurons.
source: Blue light (6.8 mW/mm2) was able to completely silence the spontaneous activity of ACR2-2A-mCherry-expressing VTAGad67+ neurons (n = 10 cells), whereas light irradiation on mCherry alone-expressing neurons had no such effect (n = 7 cells) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell-attached recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-f.

claim: Blue light illumination immediately induced wakefulness from NREM sleep in mice expressing ACR2-2A-mCherry.
source: Interestingly, blue light illumination immediately induced wakefulness from NREM sleep, but not from REM sleep, in mice expressing ACR2-2A-mCherry (n = 6 mice, Figure 3d–f, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3d-f and Video 1.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of VTAGad67+ neurons in the state of wakefulness prolonged the time spent in wakefulness to 35 ± 5 s compared to 8 ± 8 s in controls.
source: Surprisingly, we found that optogenetic inhibition of VTAGad67+ neurons in the state of wakefulness prolonged the time spent in wakefulness in all sorted trials compared to behavior of the control group (Figure 3f, ACR2: 35 ± 5 s, mCherry: 8 ± 8 s; p=0.02, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3f with statistical analysis.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of VTAGad67+ neurons can induce arousal even under conditions of high homeostatic sleep pressure following 4 hr sleep deprivation.
source: However, to our surprise, even under such a higher sleep pressure condition, optogenetic inhibition of VTAGad67+ neurons could successfully and immediately induce wakefulness in all trials (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments during recovery sleep shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: The fluorescence intensity from GCaMP6f in VTAGad67+ neurons increased in an evoked firing frequency-dependent manner.
source: The fluorescence intensity from GCaMP6f was increased in an evoked firing frequency-dependent manner (n = 13 cells; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c–e, ΔF/F (%, normalized to 100 Hz), 10 Hz: 9.2 ± 3.0, 20 Hz: 23.0 ± 5.4, 50 Hz: 52.1 ± 6.2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous calcium imaging and electrophysiology shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c-e.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons began to increase their activity before wake-to-NREM transitions.
source: Notably, VTAGad67+ neurons began to increase their activity before wake-to-NREM transitions (mean ΔF/F: Wake: 2.9 ± 0.4%, NREM: 3.8 ± 0.4%, p=2.5e-6)
evidence: This is demonstrated by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 5d.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons decrease their activity before NREM-to-REM transitions.
source: Notably, VTAGad67+ neurons began to increase their activity before wake-to-NREM transitions (mean ΔF/F: Wake: 2.9 ± 0.4%, NREM: 3.8 ± 0.4%, p=2.5e-6) and decrease their activity before NREM-to-REM (mean ΔF/F: NREM: 5.0 ± 0.5%, REM: 2.7 ± 0.3%, p=2.4e-5)
evidence: This is demonstrated by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 5d.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons decrease their activity before NREM-to-wake transitions.
source: Notably, VTAGad67+ neurons began to increase their activity before wake-to-NREM transitions (mean ΔF/F: Wake: 2.9 ± 0.4%, NREM: 3.8 ± 0.4%, p=2.5e-6) and decrease their activity before NREM-to-REM (mean ΔF/F: NREM: 5.0 ± 0.5%, REM: 2.7 ± 0.3%, p=2.4e-5) and NREM-to-wake (mean ΔF/F: NREM: 3.8 ± 0.5%, wake: 3.0 ± 0.4%, p=2.4e-4) transitions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The population activity of VTAGad67+ neurons was found to be completely contrary to DA neuronal activity in the VTA.
source: Most interestingly, the population activity of VTAGad67+ neurons was found to be completely contrary to DA neuronal activity in the VTA (Dahan et al., 2007; Eban-Rothschild et al., 2016)
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the current fiber photometry data with previously published data on DA neurons.

claim: Blue light pulses induced a post-synaptic current in 8 out of 11 orexin neurons.
source: Activation of nerve terminals of VTAGad67+ neurons in the LH (blue light pulse, duration of 5 ms) induced a post-synaptic current (PSC) in 8 out of 11 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Light-induced post-synaptic currents in orexin neurons were blocked by gabazine, a GABAA receptor antagonist.
source: These light-induced PSCs were blocked by gabazine (10 μM), a GABAA receptor antagonist (Figure 7a–c, aCSF: −253 ± 70 pA, gabazine: −9 ± 3 pA, n = 8 cells, p=1.6e-10, paired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7a-c.

claim: The average synaptic delay from light onset to post-synaptic current in orexin neurons was 6.2 ± 1.0 ms.
source: The average synaptic delay from light onset was recorded as 6.2 ± 1.0 ms (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7d.

claim: CNQX and AP5 could not block light-induced post-synaptic currents in orexin neurons.
source: CNQX and AP5 could not block light-induced PSCs, while the combination of CNQX, AP5, and gabazine could inhibit (Figure 7e–g. AP5 +CNQX: −188 ± 38 pA, with gabazine: −6 ± 2 pA, n = 7 cells, p=3.1e-9, paired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7e-g.

claim: TTX inhibited the light-induced post-synaptic currents in orexin neurons.
source: We found that tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 μM), a blocker of voltage-gated sodium channels, inhibited the light-induced PSCs (Figure 7i–k. aCSF: −340 ± 73 pA, TTX: −2 ± 0.6 pA, n = 6 cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7i-k.

claim: Combined application of TTX and 4-AP could rescue the light-induced post-synaptic currents in orexin neurons.
source: However, combined application of TTX along with 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 1 mM), a voltage-gated potassium channel blocker that prolongs depolarization of axon terminals and enables ChR2-mediated release of neurotransmitter in the absence of action potentials (Petreanu et al., 2009), could rescue the light-induced PSCs, suggesting a monosynaptic connection between VTAGad67+ neurons and LHorexin neurons (−291 ± 131 pA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7j-k.

claim: There is a monosynaptic connection between VTAGad67+ neurons and LHorexin neurons.
source: However, combined application of TTX along with 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 1 mM), a voltage-gated potassium channel blocker that prolongs depolarization of axon terminals and enables ChR2-mediated release of neurotransmitter in the absence of action potentials (Petreanu et al., 2009), could rescue the light-induced PSCs, suggesting a monosynaptic connection between VTAGad67+ neurons and LHorexin neurons (−291 ± 131 pA).
evidence: This is inferred from the TTX+4-AP rescue experiment shown in Figure 7.

claim: Blue light illumination into the LH resulted in decreased wakefulness and increased NREM sleep in ChR2-expressing mice.
source: Interestingly, blue light illumination into the LH resulted in decreased wakefulness and increased NREM sleep in the ChR2-expressing mice, whereas hrGFP-expressing mice showed no such effects (Figure 8c–e, in ChR2-expressing mice: wakefulness (in min) Pre: 55.0 ± 2.2, Stimulation: 29.2 ± 1.7, Post: 53.3 ± 2.1; p=7.3e-8 vs Pre, p=2.7e-7 vs Post, NREM (in min) Pre: 4.3 ± 1.8, Stimulation: 29.9 ± 1.8, Post: 6.0 ± 1.9, p=0 vs Pre, p=5.5e-8 vs Post, one-way ANOVA followed by post-hoc Tukey).
evidence: This is demonstrated by projection-specific optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8c-e.

claim: REM sleep remained unaffected during optogenetic activation of VTAGad67+ terminals in the LH.
source: Again, the REM sleep remained unaffected (Figure 8c–e, in ChR2-expressing mice: REM (in min) Pre: 0.7 ± 0.5, Stimulation: 0.9 ± 0.3, Post: 0.7 ± 0.4, p=0.94 vs Pre, p=0.95 vs Post, one-way ANOVA followed by post-hoc Tukey).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8c-e with statistical analysis.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons promote NREM sleep, at least in part, through their projection to the LH.
source: These results suggest that VTAGad67+ neurons promote NREM sleep, at least in part, through their projection to the LH.
evidence: This is inferred from the projection-specific optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: GABAergic neurons provide strong inhibition to the wake- and REM-active DA neurons in the VTA.
source: As GABAergic neurons provide strong inhibition to the wake- and REM-active DA neurons in the VTA (Eban-Rothschild et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eban-Rothschild et al., 2016, Tan et al., 2012, and van Zessen et al., 2012.

claim: Neurons in the rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg) are essential for physiological NREM sleep in rats.
source: Using bidirectional chemogenetic manipulations as well as neurotoxic lesions in rats, a recent study found that neurons in the rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg), also known as the GABAergic tail of the VTA, are essential for physiological NREM sleep (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: GABA neurons in the ventral medial midbrain/pons regulate sleep/wake cycles by modulating DA neurons.
source: More recently, Takata et al. reported that GABA neurons in the ventral medial midbrain/pons, which includes the VTA region, regulate sleep/wake cycles by modulating DA neurons (Takata et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takata et al., 2018.

claim: Activation of GABAergic neurons in the core of NAc or their axonal terminals in the VP evoked slow wave sleep.
source: Recently, Oishi et al. reported that activation of either the cell bodies of GABAergic neurons in the core of NAc or their axonal terminals in the VP evoked slow wave sleep (Oishi et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oishi et al., 2017b.

claim: Activation of GABAergic neurons in the basal forebrain produced wakefulness, whereas their inhibition induced sleep.
source: In addition, activation of GABAergic neurons in the basal forebrain, which includes the VP, produced wakefulness, whereas their inhibition induced sleep (Anaclet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anaclet et al., 2015.

claim: DA neurons in the VTA exhibit higher activity in REM sleep versus either wake or NREM sleep.
source: Population activity recordings across vigilance states shows that DA neurons in the VTA exhibit higher activity in REM sleep versus either wake or NREM sleep (Eban-Rothschild et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eban-Rothschild et al., 2016.

claim: In vivo single unit recordings in rats found wake- and REM-active VTAGABA neurons.
source: Using in vivo single unit recordings in rats, Lee et al. found wake- and REM-active VTAGABA neurons, suggesting that there might be several types of VTAGABA neurons (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2001.

claim: Coordinated interaction between GABA and glutamate neurons in the VTA regulates sleep/wakefulness in mice.
source: Very recently, Yu et al. reported that coordinated interaction between GABA and glutamate neurons in the VTA regulates sleep/wakefulness in mice (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2019.

claim: Selective ablation of VTAGABA neurons in rats increased spontaneous locomotor activity.
source: In addition, Shank et al. reported that dose- and time-related selective ablation of GABAergic neurons in the VTA in rats increased spontaneous locomotor activity (Shank et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shank et al., 2007.

claim: In vivo optogenetic activation of GABAergic neurons in the VTA in mice disrupts reward consummatory behavior.
source: van Zassen and colleagues reported that in vivo optogenetic activation of GABAergic neurons in the VTA in mice disrupts reward consummatory behavior (van Zessen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Zessen et al., 2012.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons projecting to the VP might be involved in the generation of slow wave sleep.
source: These facts suggest that inhibition of GABAergic neurons in the VP is a critical pathway to generate slow waves in NREM sleep. We also found that VTAGad67+ neurons moderately project to the VP. Therefore, we reasoned that VTAGad67+ neurons projecting to the VP might be involved in the generation of slow wave sleep.
evidence: This is speculated based on the projection pattern and literature on VP's role in slow wave sleep.

claim: There might be several types of VTAGABA neurons.
source: Using in vivo single unit recordings in rats, Lee et al. found wake- and REM-active VTAGABA neurons, suggesting that there might be several types of VTAGABA neurons (Lee et al., 2001). Our fiber photometry data showed that VTAGad67+ neurons exhibit weak activity even during wakefulness. This might suggest that VTAGad67+ neurons are also comprised of several subtypes.
evidence: This is inferred from the heterogeneity in activity patterns observed in different studies.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons also regulate levels of wakefulness.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of VTAGad67+ neurons prolonged wakefulness (Figure 3f). This result might suggest that VTAGad67+ neurons also regulate levels of wakefulness.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that optogenetic inhibition prolongs wakefulness.

claim: An improvement in alertness and ability to maintain wakefulness require the suppression of activity of VTAGABA neurons.
source: This is consistent with data showing that VTAGad67+ neurons displayed weak activity in wakefulness in terms of population activity. This idea is also supported by observed increases in spontaneous locomotor activity following selective ablation of VTAGABA neurons in rats (Shank et al., 2007). These facts might suggest that an improvement in alertness and ability to maintain wakefulness require the suppression of activity of VTAGABA neurons.
evidence: This is speculated based on the activity patterns and effects of ablation studies.

claim: One possible cellular mechanism underlying NREM sleep promotion by VTAGABA neurons is via inhibition of DA neurons residing in the VTA.
source: One possible cellular mechanism underlying NREM sleep promotion by VTAGABA neurons is via inhibition of DA neurons residing in the VTA.
evidence: This is speculated based on known inhibitory connections between GABAergic and DA neurons in the VTA.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons might be a possible target for therapeutic intervention in treating sleep-related as well as neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: In conclusion, our study elucidated that VTAGABA neurons regulate NREM sleep in mice. These neurons might be a possible target for therapeutic intervention in treating sleep-related as well as neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study and the known association between sleep and psychiatric disorders.

claim: Blue light inhibited LHorexin neuron firing in a light-pulse frequency-dependent manner at 5, 10 and 20 Hz.
source: We found that blue light inhibited LHorexin neuron firing in a light-pulse frequency-dependent manner (5, 10 and 20 Hz). However, no such effect was observed when yellow light pulses (20 Hz) were applied (Berndt et al., 2011) (Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loose cell-attached recordings shown in Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: Yellow light pulses at 20 Hz did not inhibit LHorexin neuron firing.
source: We found that blue light inhibited LHorexin neuron firing in a light-pulse frequency-dependent manner (5, 10 and 20 Hz). However, no such effect was observed when yellow light pulses (20 Hz) were applied (Berndt et al., 2011) (Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loose cell-attached recordings shown in Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: Blue light stimulation of 6.8 mW/mm2 increased the firing of ChR2-expressing VTAGad67+ neurons up to 674 ± 174% of baseline.
source: Blue light stimulation of 6.8 mW/mm2 increased the firing up to 674 ± 174% (n = 5 cells, p=0.004 vs both pre and post, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey post hoc tests).
evidence: This is demonstrated by current clamp recordings shown in Figure 6d-f.

claim: The calculated reversal potential of Cl- under recording conditions was near 0 mV (2.2 mV).
source: The calculated reversal potential of Cl- under recording conditions were near 0 mV (2.2 mV).
evidence: This is calculated based on the ionic composition of the recording solutions.

claim: The current direction of light-induced PSCs was opposite at +90 mV holding potential compared to -60 mV.
source: As expected, we found that the current direction of light-induced PSCs was opposite at +90 mVhold (Figure 7j–k, 237 ± 115 pA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage clamp recordings at different holding potentials shown in Figure 7j-k.

claim: LHorexin neurons were directly innervated and inhibited by VTAGad67+ neurons.
source: All these experiments confirm that LHorexin neurons were directly innervated and inhibited by VTAGad67+ neurons.
evidence: This is confirmed by multiple electrophysiology experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Faget and colleagues labeled afferent neurons to DA, GABA, or glutamate neurons in the VTA and found that these populations receive qualitatively similar inputs.
source: Using an optimized trans-synaptic retrograde tracing approach, Faget and colleagues recently labeled afferent neurons to DA, GABA, or glutamate neurons in the VTA and found that these populations receive qualitatively similar inputs, with dominant and comparable projections from three brain areas known to be critical for sleep/wakefulness regulation: LH, raphe, and ventral pallidum (Faget et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Faget et al., 2016.

claim: There exists a mutual interaction between VTAGad67+ neurons and brain areas including LH, raphe, and ventral pallidum to regulate sleep/wakefulness.
source: Here we report that VTAGad67+ neurons project to those areas, suggesting the existence of a mutual interaction with these brain areas to regulate sleep/wakefulness.
evidence: This is inferred from the projection patterns and known inputs to VTA neurons.

claim: VTAGad67+ neurons play a critical role in sleep/wakefulness-regulating circuitry as these neurons modulate diverse targets, including DA neurons in the VTA.
source: Moreover, while many brain areas including the cholinergic basal forebrain and brain stem, histaminergic posterior hypothalamus, serotonergic raphe nucleus, as well as the noradrenergic locus coeruleus are important in sleep/wake regulation (Brown et al., 2012), we speculate a critical role for VTAGad67+ neurons in sleep/wakefulness-regulating circuitry as these neurons modulate diverse targets, including DA neurons in the VTA (Tan et al., 2012).
